items.title: Aluminium 'wants' to react but doesn't
items.claim: Aluminium has a standard electrode potential of minus 1.66 V — more reactive than zinc or iron. It should fizz in water and burn in air. Yet aluminium aircraft, foil and cans sit happily for years.
items.prompt: Why doesn't aluminium corrode in air?

options.text: Pure aluminium does not react with oxygen
Aluminium instantly forms a coherent, impermeable 4 nanometre oxide layer (Al2O3) that protects the metal underneath
The factory coats aluminium with plastic before sale
Standard electrode potentials are unreliable for s and p block metals

items.reveal_title: Thermodynamics screams react! — but a passivation layer locks the door
items.reveal:
Aluminium oxide forms in milliseconds when fresh aluminium meets oxygen. Unlike iron oxide (rust), Al2O3 has almost the same molar volume as the underlying metal, so it forms a tight, adherent film. Oxygen can't reach the metal beneath, and the reaction effectively stops.

Remove the oxide (scratch it, dissolve it in alkali, or amalgamate the surface with mercury), and aluminium reacts violently. This is why aluminium powder + iron oxide (thermite) is dangerous, and why aluminium ships are vulnerable to mercury contamination.
items.why: Reactivity series is about thermodynamic tendency. Kinetics — including passivation — decides whether the reaction is observable.

items.title: Hydrogen fuel cells release energy and pure water
items.claim: A fuel cell takes hydrogen and oxygen as inputs and outputs electricity, heat and water. The overall reaction is 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O — the same as combustion — but it produces electrical work directly, with efficiency up to about 60 percent (vs about 25 percent for a typical petrol engine).
items.prompt: Why is a fuel cell more efficient than a heat engine?

options.text: Fuel cells convert chemical energy directly to electrical work, bypassing the Carnot limit that constrains heat engines; combustion engines must go via heat first, losing efficiency
Fuel cells use catalysts not available to engines

items.reveal:
Combustion engines convert chemical energy → heat → mechanical work. Carnot's limit caps the efficiency: 1 - Tcold/Thot. With realistic temperatures (Tcold ~ 300 K, Thot ~ 2000 K), the theoretical maximum is about 85 percent — and real engines do far worse because of irreversibilities.

Fuel cells convert chemical energy → electrical work directly. They are limited by the Gibbs free energy change, not the Carnot ratio. For H2 + 1/2 O2 → H2O, delta G is about 237 kJ/mol while delta H is 286 kJ/mol — so the theoretical maximum efficiency is delta G / delta H = 83 percent.

In practice, the hard part is cost and durability of platinum-group catalysts and managing membrane water balance. Hydrogen storage is also a major engineering challenge.
items.why: Fuel cells are presented as 'clean'. The deeper point is that they sidestep the thermodynamic limit that handicaps combustion engines.

items.title: An atom is about 99.9999999999999 percent empty space
items.claim: If a hydrogen atom were scaled up so the nucleus was the size of a marble (1 cm), the electron would orbit roughly 1 kilometre away. Almost everything 'solid' around you is overwhelmingly empty.
items.prompt: If atoms are mostly empty, why does a wall feel solid?

options.text: Walls have very few atoms in them
Solidity comes from electromagnetic repulsion between electron clouds and from Pauli exclusion preventing electron states from overlapping — not from particles physically touching
Atoms swell up to fill space when forces are applied
The 'empty space' is filled with a dense medium

items.reveal:
A hydrogen atom is about 10 to the minus 10 m across. Its nucleus is about 10 to the minus 15 m. The ratio is 100,000 — so atoms are about 10 to the 15 times more volume than nuclei.

When you touch a table, no atoms touch. Electromagnetic forces between the electron clouds of your fingertip and the wood push back. The Pauli exclusion principle prevents the electrons from sharing identical quantum states, contributing the actual 'incompressibility' of matter.

Rutherford's 1909 gold foil experiment showed this directly — most alphas passed through gold foil unscathed because gold atoms are mostly empty.
items.why: Students treat atoms as small spheres of stuff. They are tiny dense nuclei surrounded by enormous shells of probability.
